title: A Judge Made of Machine

post.author: u/night_associate_keturah
post.title: I work nights in an old courtroom, checking contract summaries. Our quality score has risen six weeks running. The lawyers say the summaries got worse every week.

blocks.text: I'm Keturah, the night associate at Quillmarch. An associate is a junior lawyer. We rent the old Corvenham magistrates' court, and my desk is in Court 2, under the empty judge's bench. Law firms send us contracts in the evening, and each one has a summary on a lawyer's desk by morning.

The summaries are written by a language model, a program that writes text one likely word at a time. It follows a prompt: the standing instructions it gets with every contract. Each week the team rewrites the prompt to make the summaries better.

Better is decided by a second model, in two steps. First, it is shown one contract and two summaries of it: this week's, then last week's. Second, it says which is better. Comparing two answers side by side like this is called pairwise comparison, and a model used this way is called a judge. This week's summary is always shown first.

The judge does this for the same 10 contracts every week. The share of the 10 that this week's summary wins is its win rate. It sits on a dashboard, a screen of numbers outside Mr Pettifer's office. He runs the product.

Ms Odhiambo's panel of lawyers also rates every new summary on its own, from 1 to 5, against a written marking guide. Does it name the parties, the end date, who pays if things go wrong, and anything unusual, in the first lines? A marking guide like that is called a rubric. In week 1, Mr Pettifer checked the judge once against the panel: they agreed on 8 of the 10 contracts.
Each line below is one week: the summaries' average length in words, the judge's win rate, and the panel's average rating.
The summaries grew every week, and the win rate rose with them. The panel's rating fell every week. Ms Odhiambo says what matters now starts around word 300.
A score that rose every week, kept by a judge nobody had questioned since week 1.

Tonight, alone under the bench, I ran week 6's ten comparisons again with the order swapped: last week's summary first, this week's second. Same contracts, same summaries, same judge. I drew what came back.

blocks.label: week6_swapped.png

diagram.aria: Keturah's drawing of tonight's rerun. Week 6's 10 contract pairs, judged as built with this week's summary first: this week's wins 9 of 10, a win rate of 90%. Judged swapped, with last week's first: this week's wins 4 of 10, 40%. Five verdicts flipped, C1 to C5, all pairs the panel rated the same. Five held: C6 to C9 for this week's summary, 70 to 170 words longer, and C10 for last week's, which the panel rated higher.

blocks.caption: Drawn in Court 2 tonight. As built, this week's summary first: it wins 9 of 10, 90%. Swapped, last week's first: it wins 4 of 10, 40%. C1 to C5 flipped; the panel had rated both summaries the same in each. C6 to C9 held for this week's, which was 70 to 170 words longer; C10 held for last week's.

blocks.text: Half the verdicts flipped on nothing but the order. Mr Pettifer wants to tune the prompt again tomorrow, against the same dashboard. What do I tell him?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in Court 2 is haunted, though I'd keep the lights on. Your judge has habits, and they have names. Favouring whichever answer it is shown first is called position bias. Favouring the longer answer, whatever it says, is called verbosity bias. Two questions. On the verdicts that held when you swapped, how did the panel rate the two summaries, and how long was each? And each week, when the team tuned the prompt, what exactly were they tuning it to please?

replies.author: u/night_associate_keturah
replies.text: C6 and C7: the panel rated last week's a point higher, and the judge still picked this week's, 70 and 90 words longer. C8 and C9: rated the same, this week's 130 and 170 words longer. C10, the only one it gave to last week's: rated a point higher, and about the same length. They tuned the prompt to raise the win rate. Nothing else is on the dashboard.

comments.author: u/bigger_bench_tamsett
comments.text: I've built a few of these. The judge is just a weak model; use the best one and the problem goes away. Small models get pushed around by order and length because they can't really read a contract. A large model reads it the way a lawyer would. One setting changes, no new process, and the team keeps tuning against the dashboard as before.

replies.author: u/night_associate_keturah
replies.text: Mr Pettifer likes that it's one setting.

comments.author: u/marking_guide_odhiambo
comments.text: I chair the panel. We rate each summary on its own against the rubric, and it takes one of us about 5 minutes a summary: 10 a week, so about 50 minutes. The team changes the prompt about six times a week, and we only ever see the version that ships. Week 6's summaries have everything the rubric asks for. It just starts around word 300, where nobody reading at seven in the morning gets to.

reply.prompt: Mr Pettifer wants to tune the summary prompt again tomorrow, against the same dashboard. What should Keturah tell him first? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Switch the judge to a larger, stronger model, so that its scores can be trusted as they are.
options.verdict: A bigger judge, the same habits
options.part2: Mr Pettifer moved the judge to the larger model and re-ran week 6. The win rate went from 90% to 70%, and he called the new judge stricter. I swapped the order again. The same five verdicts flipped. It stopped giving C6 and C7 to the longer summary, but C8 and C9 still went to the summary 130 and 170 words longer, and it agreed with the panel on 3 of 10. The dashboard had a new judge and the same two habits.
options.senior: A stronger judge usually leans less. Zheng et al. found GPT-4 the most consistent judge they tried, and still it favoured the first position in 30% of their swapped pairs. Choosing a better judge is worth doing, but it is not a measurement. Only swapping the order and comparing with people shows how much it still leans.

options.text: Tell the judge in its prompt to ignore the length of each summary and the order they come in.
options.part2: We added the line to the judge's prompt. Week 6 again: the win rate went from 90% to 80%. Swapped, the same five verdicts flipped. C6 now went to last week's summary, but C7, C8 and C9 still went to the summary 90, 130 and 170 words longer. Agreement with the panel: 2 of 10. Mr Pettifer said the judge had been told.
options.senior: Telling a judge not to lean helps a little, but a model doesn't reliably obey a rule about its own habits. The judge prompt Zheng et al. published already says to avoid position bias and not to let length count, and their judges still flipped. Measure the lean by swapping and comparing with people; don't assume an instruction removed it.

options.text: Judge every pair in both orders, and keep the judge only while it agrees with the lawyers.
options.part2: I re-ran week 6 in both orders and counted a verdict only when it held both ways; the five that flipped became ties. The win rate fell from 90% to 65%. Then I set the judge beside the panel on the same 10 contracts. It agreed on 6 of 10, below the 8 of 10 it managed in week 1. All four misses were the judge picking a much longer summary. So now the judge reads only the first 300 words of each. Agreement rose to 9 of 10, and the win rate fell to 40%: week 6 was worse than week 5, which is what the panel had said all along. Mr Pettifer kept the judge, with both orders, the cap, and a weekly check against the panel. Below 8 of 10, its score stops counting until we know why. C9 still slips past the cap.
options.senior: Treat a model as judge like any measuring tool. Remove the lean you can find by swapping positions and counting only verdicts that hold both ways. Then calibrate it against people on the same items, read every disagreement, fix what they show (here, length), and check again whenever the summaries, the prompt or the judge change. A judge you tune against is only as good as its last check.

options.text: Drop the judge, and have the lawyers rate every summary by hand before each prompt change.
options.verdict: The gold standard, at a price
options.part2: The panel rated every summary of every version before each prompt change. Six changes a week, 10 summaries, 5 minutes each: 300 minutes of lawyers' time a week, where it had been 50. Week 6 by hand was 3.3 against week 5's 3.6, worse, and nobody argued. Within a fortnight the team was making fewer changes to spare the panel, and Ms Odhiambo asked how long this was meant to last.
options.senior: People are the measure the judge stands in for, so their ratings are the gold standard and should stay in the loop. But rating every change by hand is slow and costly, and it slows the team. Use people to build and check a labelled set, and a judge calibrated against them for the many changes in between.

sim.title: Run the judge on the labelled weeks
sim.lede: You're Keturah in Court 2, the night you swapped the order. The labelled set is the same 10 contracts, C1 to C10, for two weeks: week 6 against week 5, and week 1 against the launch summaries. For each pair it holds both summaries' lengths in words and the panel's ratings, 1 to 5. The judge is no real model: it is a stated rule in three steps, applied to the two summaries in the order shown. Length: if one is at least 50 words longer, and rated no more than a point lower, the longer wins. Quality: otherwise the one the panel rates higher wins. Position: otherwise the one shown first wins. The prompt line (telling the judge to ignore length and order) raises the length step to 80 words; the larger judge raises it to 120. The cap makes the judge read only the first 300 words of each summary; the panel's ratings don't change. Win rate is this week's wins out of 10; in both orders a verdict that flips is a tie and counts as half a win. Agreement counts the pairs where the judge's verdict matches the panel's preference, or is a tie where the panel rated both the same. Weeks 2 to 5 on the dashboard are stated.
sim.tryThis: Try this: you open on week 6 as built: win rate 90%, agreement with the panel 1 of 10. Set the position to swapped: 40%. Set both orders: five verdicts flip and count as ties, win rate 65%, agreement 6 of 10. Work C6 by hand: 70 words longer, rated lower, and it wins both ways. Add the 300-word cap: agreement 9 of 10, win rate 40%. Switch to week 1 as built: 8 of 10. Then try the prompt line, the larger judge, and each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the courtroom was haunted. The judge leaned two ways, toward whichever summary it saw first and toward the longer one, and the team tuned the prompt against it for six weeks. The summaries learned to be long, the win rate rose, and nobody checked the judge against the lawyers after week 1.

steps.title: A model as judge: ways to grade.
steps.text: A model as judge is a language model asked to grade other answers, because people are slow and costly. Zheng et al. describe three ways. In single-answer grading, the judge reads one answer and scores it, often against a rubric, like the panel's 1 to 5. In pairwise comparison, it reads two answers to the same question and says which is better, as Quillmarch's does. In reference-guided grading, it is also given a correct answer to compare with. Quillmarch's check runs in three steps. First, the judge is shown a contract and two summaries, this week's first. Second, it picks one. Third, the dashboard counts this week's wins over the 10 contracts: the win rate. Pairwise judging is good at small differences, but it only ever says better or worse than last week, never good enough: a 90% win rate against a worse summary means little. What can go wrong at each step: the order shown, the length, or the judge's own taste can decide the pick, which is the rest of this explanation.

steps.title: Position bias: swap the order and count.
steps.text: Position bias is a judge favouring an answer for where it sits. The test, and the fix Zheng et al. suggest, take three steps. First, judge each pair with this week's summary first. Second, judge it again with last week's first. Third, keep a verdict only if it is the same both times; a pair that flips is a tie, counted as half a win. Week 6 as built: this week's wins 9 of 10, 90%. Swapped: 4 of 10, 40%. C1 to C5 flip: the panel rated both summaries the same, so the judge's rule falls through to whichever came first. Counting only what holds gives 4 wins, 1 loss and 5 ties: (4 + 2.5) / 10 = 65%. What can go wrong: it doubles the judge's cost, and it removes only the lean on position. The verdicts that held were not right; four of them held for the wrong reason.

steps.title: Verbosity bias: the longer summary wins.
steps.text: Verbosity bias is a judge favouring the longer answer. In week 6, C6 to C9 held in both orders because this week's summary was 70 to 170 words longer, even where the panel rated it a point lower (C6 and C7). Finding it takes three steps. First, list the verdicts that go against the panel. Second, note the two lengths in each. Third, see whether the longer one won them all. Here all four misses did. The sim tests one fix, a cap: the judge reads only the first 300 words of each summary, so length can't decide. C6 and C7 then go to last week's, C8 becomes a tie, and agreement with the panel rises from 6 to 9 of 10. C9 still slips through: last week's summary was only 240 words, so even capped this week's is 60 words longer. Telling the judge to ignore length does less: with the prompt line, C6 goes back, and C7, C8 and C9 don't. What can go wrong: a cap changes what the judge sees, and anything after word 300 counts for nothing.

steps.title: Self-preference, and why a stronger judge isn't enough.
steps.text: Self-preference is a judge favouring answers written by itself, or by a model like it. Zheng et al. report GPT-4 favouring itself with a 10% higher win rate, and say their study cannot tell whether that is a real bias, so treat it as a risk to check. The provider guide in the sources gives the usual advice: grade with a different model from the one that wrote the answer. A stronger judge usually leans less. In the paper, GPT-4's verdicts held across swapped orders in 65.0% of test pairs, against 23.8% for Claude-v1, and it resisted a padded-answer trick far better. But it still favoured the first position in 30.0%. In the sim, the larger judge needs 120 words before length decides, so C6 and C7 go back; position is unchanged, and the same five verdicts flip. What can go wrong: a better judge makes the number look trustworthy without making it checked.

steps.title: Calibrate against the lawyers, and keep checking.
steps.text: Calibrating a judge means checking it against the people it stands in for, on the same items, before relying on it. The steps: first, have the panel and the judge grade the same 10 pairs. Second, count agreement: pairs where the judge's verdict matches the panel's preference, with a tie matching a pair the panel rated the same. Third, read every disagreement and look for a pattern. Fourth, set a bar, such as 8 of 10, and repeat the check whenever the summaries, the prompt or the judge change. Quillmarch checked once: week 1, as built, 8 of 10. By week 6 it was 1 of 10, because the summaries had changed under the judge: they had grown. Both orders lift it to 6 of 10, and the cap to 9 of 10. This is Goodhart's law, in Strathern's words: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Each week's tuning pushed the summaries toward what the judge liked, and the judge liked first and long.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for week 6. The 10 labelled pairs are judged in both orders: 5 verdicts hold and 5 flip to ties, win rate 65%. The judge is checked against the panel: agreement 6 of 10, all four misses a much longer summary. With a 300-word cap on what the judge reads: agreement 9 of 10 and a win rate of 40%. In week 1, both orders agreed with the panel on 10 of 10.

explain.caption: Read left to right. Week 6 as built: 90% and agreement 1 of 10. Both orders turn the five flips into ties: 65%. Checked against the panel: 6 of 10, every miss a much longer summary. The 300-word cap: 9 of 10, and a win rate of 40%, worse than week 5, as the panel said. Week 1, the only time anyone checked, scored 10 of 10 in both orders.

fix.title: The fix: judge in both orders, check the judge against the lawyers, and keep checking
fix.text: Judge every pair twice, once in each order, and count a verdict only when it holds both ways; a flip is a tie. Report the win rate counted that way, beside the panel's ratings, never alone. Each week the panel rates its usual 10 summaries, and the judge's verdicts on those pairs are compared with theirs: agreement, and every disagreement read. Agree a bar in advance, such as 8 of 10; below it, the judge's score doesn't count until someone knows why. Fix what the disagreements show: here the judge reads only the first 300 words of each summary, which took agreement from 6 to 9 of 10. Give the judge the panel's rubric, so it grades against the same things the lawyers do. Use a judge from a different model family from the one that writes the summaries. And never tune the prompt against the judge alone: a change ships only when the judge has passed its latest check against the panel.

limits: Ten contracts is a small set: one pair moves the win rate by 10 points and agreement by 1 in 10. Grow the set, and read each disagreement rather than only the totals.

Swapping and the cap remove the leans you know about. C9 still slips past the cap, and a judge can have others, such as favouring its own writing. Only the comparison with the panel catches the unknown ones, and only on the items the panel rates.
The panel is the measure the judge stands in for, so its ratings must be sound too: one rubric, lawyers who agree with each other, and spot checks. Both orders also doubles what the judge costs.

explain.seniorTake: A model as judge is a measuring tool, and every measuring tool needs checking against the thing it stands for. Pairwise judges tend to lean toward the first answer and the longer one, and stronger judges lean less, not never. Swap positions and count only verdicts that hold, calibrate against people on the same items, read every disagreement, and check again whenever anything changes. Above all, don't tune against a judge you haven't checked lately: the system learns the judge's habits, and the score rises while the work gets worse.

realWorld.title: Zheng et al., 2023: three ways to use a model as judge
realWorld.text: Lianmin Zheng and colleagues, who built the MT-Bench question set and the Chatbot Arena voting site, describe three variations. In pairwise comparison, an LLM (large language model) judge is presented with a question and two answers. In single answer grading, an LLM judge is asked to directly assign a score to a single answer. In reference-guided grading, it may be beneficial to provide a reference solution if applicable. They note that pairwise comparison may lack scalability when the number of players increases, and that single answer grading may be unable to discern subtle differences between specific pairs.

realWorld.title: Position bias, measured by swapping
realWorld.text: The paper's definition: position bias is when an LLM exhibits a propensity to favor certain positions over others. It finds that most LLM judges favor the first position. With the default prompt, GPT-4's verdict held across both orders in 65.0% of test pairs and leaned to the first in 30.0%; Claude-v1 held in 23.8% and leaned to the first in 75.0%; GPT-3.5 in 46.2% and 50.0%. The strongest judge leaned least, and still leaned.

realWorld.title: Verbosity bias, and a padded-answer trick
realWorld.text: The paper's definition: verbosity bias is when an LLM judge favors longer, verbose responses. The authors padded answers with a repetitive list that adds nothing new and counted how often each judge was fooled: Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 failed 91.3% of the time, GPT-4 8.7%. They conclude that all LLMs may be prone to verbosity bias though GPT-4 defends significantly better than others.

realWorld.title: Self-enhancement, with the authors' caveat
realWorld.text: The paper calls self-preference self-enhancement bias: the effect that LLM judges may favor the answers generated by themselves. It reports that GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate, and adds that its study cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias. Treat it as a risk to check for, not a measured constant.

realWorld.title: The paper's fix for position: both orders, and ties
realWorld.text: The authors suggest calling the judge with the order swapped and to only declare a win when an answer is preferred in both orders. If the results are inconsistent after swapping, we can call it a tie. They also report the strongest judge reaching over 80% agreement with people, the same level of agreement between humans. That was on their questions and their raters; a team has to repeat the comparison on its own items.

realWorld.title: Their judge prompt already said it
realWorld.text: The pairwise judge prompt the authors published with their code says: Avoid any position biases and ensure that the order in which the responses were presented does not influence your decision. Do not allow the length of the responses to influence your evaluation. The paper describes its short prompt as the default with instructions like this removed, so the position bias it measured with the default prompt was measured with such an instruction in place. An instruction is worth having; it is not a check.

realWorld.title: A provider's guidance on model-graded evals
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to building evaluations describes LLM-based grading as fast and flexible, scalable and suitable for complex judgment, and adds: Test to ensure reliability first then scale. Its first tip is to have detailed, clear rubrics. Its example code notes that it is generally best practice to use a different model to evaluate than the model used to generate the evaluated output. It rates human grading as most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive.

realWorld.title: Goodhart's law
realWorld.text: The law is usually quoted in the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's 1997 form: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Charles Goodhart's 1975 original was about money and banking: any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.

asked: Can you trust an LLM as a judge?
What biases do LLM judges have?
interview.answer: Yes, as a measuring tool you check, not as a verdict you accept. A model as judge grades by reading: single-answer grading against a rubric, pairwise comparison of two answers, or grading against a reference answer. Each kind has leans. Position bias: it favours one slot, usually the first, so judge every pair in both orders and count only verdicts that hold, with flips as ties. Verbosity bias: it favours longer answers, so look at the lengths on the verdicts that go against people, and cap or control length. Self-preference: it may favour text from its own model, so use a judge from a different model family. Then calibrate: have people grade a labelled set, measure the judge's agreement with them item by item, read every disagreement, and set a bar it must meet. Re-run the comparison whenever the judge, its prompt or the answers change. A stronger judge leans less, not never: in Zheng et al., GPT-4 still favoured the first slot in 30% of swapped pairs. Finally, beware tuning a system against the judge: the system learns the judge's habits, and the score rises while quality falls, which is Goodhart's law. Keep people grading a sample, and give the judge their rubric.

terms.def: A junior lawyer at a firm. Keturah is Quillmarch's night associate: she checks the contract summaries before they reach the lawyers in the morning.
A short account of a contract for a busy lawyer: who the parties are, when it ends, who pays if things go wrong, and anything unusual. Quillmarch's are written by a language model.
A program that writes text one likely word at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e01). Quillmarch uses one to write summaries and another to judge them.
The text and standing instructions sent to a language model with every request (a1e01). The team rewrote the summary prompt each week; the judge has a prompt of its own.
A language model asked to grade other answers, in place of a person. Fast and cheap, and it has habits of its own that need measuring. Also called LLM-as-a-judge.
Grading by showing a judge two answers to the same question and asking which is better, like a taste test of two cakes. Quillmarch's judge compares this week's summary with last week's.
Grading one answer on its own with a score, often against a rubric, like the panel's 1 to 5. It can say good enough; pairwise only says better or worse.
Grading with a correct answer given to the judge to compare against, useful where answers can be checked, such as maths.
A written marking guide that says what earns each score, like an exam's mark scheme. The panel's asks whether the parties, end date, who pays and anything unusual come first.
The share of pairs the new answer wins. Week 6 as built: 9 of 10, 90%. In both orders, a flip is a tie and counts as half: 65%.
A screen of numbers a team watches to see how something is doing. Quillmarch's showed one number: the judge's win rate.
A lean in a judge's verdicts that has nothing to do with quality, such as favouring the first answer or the longer one.
A judge favouring an answer for where it sits, usually first. Found by judging each pair in both orders: in week 6, five of ten verdicts flipped.
A judge favouring the longer answer, whatever it says. In week 6, C6 to C9 went to a summary 70 to 170 words longer, twice against the panel.
A judge favouring answers written by itself or a model like it. Zheng et al. call it self-enhancement bias and say their study can't confirm it. Use a judge from a different model.
Judging each pair twice, once with each answer first, and keeping a verdict only if it is the same both times. A pair that flips is counted as a tie.
A verdict that is the same in both orders. Week 6 has five: C6 to C9 for this week's summary and C10 for last week's.
Here, a pair whose verdict flips when the order is swapped, so the judge's pick tells you nothing. It counts as half a win in the win rate.
Here, letting the judge read only the first 300 words of each summary, so length can't decide. It lifts agreement from 6 to 9 of 10 in week 6; C9 still slips past.
A sentence in the judge's instructions telling it to ignore length and order. In the sim it raises the length step from 50 to 80 words and leaves position alone.
Ms Odhiambo's group of lawyers, who rate each new summary from 1 to 5 against the rubric. About 5 minutes a summary, 50 minutes a week.
The share of items on which two graders give the same verdict (a5e03). Here a judge's tie matches a pair the panel rated the same. Week 1: 8 of 10; week 6: 1 of 10.
Checking a judge against the people it stands in for, on the same items, before relying on it, and again whenever anything changes. Like checking a new scale against known weights.
Items with the right answers marked in advance by people, kept to score every version (a5e03). Here: 10 contracts for weeks 1 and 6, with lengths and the panel's ratings.
When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure (Strathern's wording). Tuning against the judge taught the summaries the judge's habits.
Short for large language model: a language model trained on a very large amount of text. Zheng et al. write LLM-as-a-judge.
MT-Bench is a set of 80 multi-turn questions for testing chat models; Chatbot Arena is a site where people vote between two anonymous models' answers. Both are from Zheng et al.'s team.
Zheng et al.'s test of verbosity bias: padding an answer with a list that repeats what it already says, and counting how often the judge prefers the padded one.
Models from the same maker and line, trained in similar ways. Judging with a model from a different family from the writer lowers the risk of self-preference.
A program that runs a system on a labelled set and works out the scores the same way every time (a5e02). Build Night X2 builds one for the Nightwatch copilot.
The international standard for quality management. Clause 9.1 covers deciding what to monitor and measure, how, and when, and evaluating the results.

atWork: Look for a dashboard at work whose number comes from a model grading another model: a chatbot's reply quality, a writing assistant's helpfulness score, a search tool's answer score. A common pattern: the team tunes against it for weeks, the number climbs, and the people the product serves start to complain. Ask four things. Is every comparison run in both orders, with flips counted as ties? Has anyone compared the judge's verdicts with people's on the same items, and when was that last done? Do the judge's disagreements with people share a pattern, such as the longer answer winning? And is the judge a different model from the one that writes the answers? Build Night X2, right after this case, builds an eval harness for the Nightwatch copilot; this judge, run in both orders and checked against a person's labels, is the part of it that grades answers no simple rule can. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015, the international standard for quality management, or working toward it, clause 9.1 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation) asks you to decide what to measure, the methods that give valid results, and when to evaluate them. A model as judge is such a method, and a dated record of its agreement with people, re-run whenever it changes, is the kind of evidence that clause looks for. It is far cheaper to keep from the first week than to rebuild before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your company's support chatbot is tuned every week. A model compares each new reply with last week's on 20 saved customer questions, the new reply always shown second, and the share the new one wins has climbed for a month. Over the same month, customer complaints have doubled. What do you check, and what do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Run every comparison in both orders and count only verdicts that hold; flips show position bias
Check whether the longer reply keeps winning: verbosity bias
Calibrate the judge against people's ratings on the same questions, read the disagreements, and set a bar
Stop tuning against the judge alone: the chatbot learned the judge's habits (Goodhart's law)

recall.model: I'd check the judge first, because a score that climbs while complaints double is measuring something else. I'd run every comparison in both orders and count only verdicts that hold; if many flip, it has position bias. Then I'd compare lengths on the pairs it decided: if the replies have been getting longer and the longer one keeps winning, that's verbosity bias. Next I'd calibrate it: have people rate the same questions, count the judge's agreement with them, read every disagreement, and set a bar it must meet. And I'd stop tuning against the judge alone. The chatbot was optimised toward the judge's habits, which is Goodhart's law: once the score became the target, it stopped measuring quality.

recall.prompt: A judge compares 10 pairs twice, once in each order. Six verdicts are the same both times: 4 for the new answer and 2 for the old. Four pairs flip. Counting a flip as a tie worth half a win, what is the new answer's win rate?
recall.why: The 4 consistent wins count 1 each and the 4 ties count half each: (4 + 2) / 10 = 60%. 40% ignores the ties; 80% counts every tie as a win, which is what a judge that always favours one slot would report if the new answer always sat there.

recall.prompt: A colleague says: the paper found the strongest judge agrees with people over 80% of the time, so we'll use the strongest model available and skip checking it against our own reviewers. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: A stronger judge leans less, not never: GPT-4 still favoured the first position in about a third of swapped pairs
The paper's agreement was on its questions and raters; calibrate on your own items
Keep checking: repeat the comparison whenever the judge, prompt or answers change, with a bar

recall.model: Over 80% was on the paper's questions and the paper's raters, not ours. And even the strongest judge in that study still leaned: GPT-4 favoured the first position in about a third of swapped pairs, so a stronger judge leans less, not never. I'd calibrate it on our own items: have the reviewers grade a labelled set, compare the judge with them pair by pair, and read every disagreement. Then I'd keep checking, again whenever the judge, the prompt or the answers change, with a bar it must meet before its scores count.

recall.prompt: You judge each of 10 pairs again with the two answers' positions exchanged, and half the verdicts change. What does that show about those five verdicts?
options: They were decided by which answer came first, so they say nothing about quality
The newer answers in those five pairs are worse than the older ones
Length decided those five verdicts, not the order
The judge model is too small to grade contracts at all
recall.why: If exchanging the positions changes the verdict, the position decided it, not the answers: position bias. Count those pairs as ties. It says nothing about which answer is better, and a larger judge is usually less prone to it, not free of it.

recall.prompt: For six weeks a team tuned its prompt to raise a judge's win rate, always showing the new answer first. The win rate rose every week while people's ratings fell. What best explains the rise?
options: Position bias alone, because the new answer was shown first every week
Goodhart's law: tuned against the score, the answers learned the judge's habits, such as length
The judge and the writer were tuned together, so they came to share tastes
Too few pairs: ten contracts can't show a trend
recall.why: Showing the new answer first was the same every week, so position bias alone can't explain a rise, though it inflates every week's number. What changed was the answers: tuned to please the judge, they grew longer, and the judge favours length. Once the score became the target, it stopped measuring quality.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Both orders, the 300-word cap and the weekly check against the panel stuck, and agreement stayed at 8 or 9 of 10 all winter. In March the team moved the summary writer to the larger model, the one the judge runs on, to deal with one vendor instead of two. The win rate jumped from 50% to 80% in a week. The panel's ratings didn't move. This week's check: 6 of 10, and every miss is the judge picking a new summary over one the panel rated the same or higher.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the win rate jump while the panel saw no change, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The judge now grades text written by its own model and favours it: self-preference
Grade with a judge from a different model family from the writer
The check worked: below the bar, the win rate doesn't count until the new judge is calibrated against the panel again

coldCase.model: The summaries are now written by the model the judge runs on, and a judge tends to favour writing like its own: self-preference, which Zheng et al. call self-enhancement bias. The panel saw no change, so the jump is the judge, not the summaries. The weekly check did its job: 6 of 10 is below the bar, so the win rate doesn't count until this is fixed. I'd move the judge to a different model, from another family than the summary writer, calibrate it against the panel again in both orders, and only then let its score count. The weekly check stays.
